title: Define success metrics for mixed-workload scheduler tail latency improvements (Hosted vs Dedicated)
creator: Lauren Bishop
project: Mixed-workload scheduler prototype (Serving Runtime Performance: Kernel + Scheduling)
description:
Context
- We are prototyping a short/long prompt-aware scheduling policy in the serving runtime to reduce p95 tail latency under mixed prompt-length distributions (short chat prompts interleaved with long-context requests).
- PM asks: align what “success” means across Hosted API and Dedicated, agree on acceptable throughput trade-offs, and define how we communicate results internally (eng leadership, SRE, releases, GTM).

Problem statement
- Today, mixed workloads can cause head-of-line blocking (long-prefill / long-context dominating GPU scheduling) which inflates p95 for latency-sensitive short prompts. Customers experience this as TTFT spikes and “chat feels slow,” even when average throughput looks fine.
- Engineering needs clear, measurable go/no-go metrics that balance user-perceived latency, overall throughput, and fairness (no long-request starvation).

Goal
- Produce a single, shared scorecard for the canary decision and graduation criteria, with separate sections for Hosted vs Dedicated that reflect different expectations (SLO posture, isolation, contract/SLA, and customer comms).

Definitions (to avoid metric confusion)
- TTFT: time to first token (user-perceived responsiveness).
- End-to-end latency: request start to final token.
- Queue time: time spent waiting in scheduler/queues before GPU service.
- Prefill latency: time spent in prefill stage.
- Decode latency: time spent in decode stage.
- Throughput: tokens/sec at pool level (and optionally requests/sec for standard scenarios).
- Fairness/Progress: guarantees that long requests continue to make progress under sustained short traffic.

Proposed success criteria (primary)
A) Hosted API (default pools)
1) Tail latency improvement for short prompts in mixed traffic
- Primary: p95 TTFT for “short class” improves by >= 15% vs baseline on representative mixed scenarios (80/20 short/long and long-spike) at comparable load.
- Secondary: p95 end-to-end latency for short class improves by >= 10%.
2) Guardrail: no material regression for long prompts
- p95 TTFT for “long class” does not regress by > 10% vs baseline.
- p99 end-to-end latency for long class does not regress by > 15% (flag for review; not automatic rollback unless combined with SRE guardrails).
3) Guardrail: throughput and error
- Pool-level tokens/sec does not regress by > 3% on steady-state mixes (80/20 and 50/50) at target utilization bands.
- Error rate (5xx, timeouts) does not regress; SRE to define thresholds per region/pool.

B) Dedicated (contracted pools)
1) Tail latency improvement OR predictability improvement
- Primary: p95 TTFT for short class improves by >= 10% OR variance reduces (measured as p95/p50 ratio for TTFT improves by >= 10%) under customer-representative mixed mixes.
2) Stronger fairness requirement
- No starvation events in canary window. “Starvation event” defined as any long-class request waiting time exceeding max(60s, 10x its baseline p95 queue time) OR starvation counter > 0 for > 5 consecutive minutes.
3) Throughput trade-off tolerance (Dedicated only)
- Accept up to 5% throughput regression if tail latency improves and customer-facing SLA/SLO posture remains within contract bounds. Any regression > 5% requires explicit approval from Runtime Eng sponsor (Mateo) + Dedicated PM (Lauren) + SRE sponsor (Sean).

Proposed success criteria (secondary / diagnostic)
- Queue time for short class: p95 queue time reduced by >= 20% in mixed scenarios.
- Scheduler stability: kernel selection thrash incidents = 0 in perf-canary runs (qualitative review from kernels team).
- Skew control: dispatch share stays within configured bounds; no sustained “all short” servicing that causes long backlog growth.

Benchmarking / evidence required for go/no-go
- Benchmark lab runs:
  - Mixed workload scenarios: 80/20 short/long, 50/50, and long-spike.
  - Models: top 2–3 production models for chat + at least one long-context heavy model.
  - Hardware: representative SKU(s) used for Hosted default pools + at least one Dedicated-heavy SKU.
- Trace replay:
  - Replay anonymized production traces when available, focusing on periods that historically show p95 spikes.
- Perf-canary:
  - Nightly job must show no regression for 3 consecutive nights on mixed scenarios before production ramp (unless waived due to urgent customer escalation).

Decision / graduation rubric
- Green (graduate to broader canary): Meets Hosted criteria A1 + A3, and Dedicated criteria B2; no SRE rollback triggers hit.
- Yellow (iterate): Improves short TTFT but violates throughput guardrail or long-class regression guardrail; proceed only with parameter tuning and rerun benchmarks.
- Red (rollback): SRE rollback triggers hit during canary OR starvation events observed OR throughput regression > tolerance.

How we will communicate results internally
1) Single source of truth
- Confluence page: “Mixed-workload scheduler prototype – Success metrics & scorecard (PM-612)” linked from ENG-2417.
- Include:
  - Final metric definitions
  - Pass/fail thresholds
  - Current status vs thresholds
  - Open questions and agreed exceptions
2) Weekly update cadence
- Post weekly scorecard snapshot in #eng-runtime and #eng-sre (short template).
- Send a brief summary to #eng-releases ahead of any canary ramp.
3) Canary decision meeting
- 30-min go/no-go with Runtime Scheduling TL (Lena), SRE sponsor (Sean), Dedicated PM (Lauren), Hosted PM (Nikhil), release coordinator (Connor).
- Output: written decision + next steps, posted as Linear update and linked in Confluence.

Open questions (need alignment)
- What is the “short vs long” cutoff for reporting? (Engineering may tune threshold; PM asks that metrics be reported by class as implemented, and additionally by absolute prompt length buckets for comparability.)
- Do we report per-model or roll up? Proposal: per-model for the top 3, plus a weighted rollup across top traffic.
- Dedicated: should we require explicit opt-in per customer pool even during internal canary? (Lean yes; coordinate via rollout plan ENG-2470.)

Acceptance criteria
- Confluence scorecard drafted and reviewed by Runtime Scheduling (Sofia/Lena), SRE (Sean/Aisha), and Dedicated PM (Lauren).
- Clear numeric thresholds for:
  - Hosted p95 TTFT improvement target
  - Throughput regression guardrail
  - Long-class regression guardrail
  - Starvation definition
- Agreement on comms template and decision cadence.

Links / references
- Linear initiative: sources/linear/engineering/ENG-2417-mixed-workload-scheduler-prototype-initiative.json
- Benchmark suite task: sources/linear/engineering/ENG-2449-add-mixed-workload-benchmarks-to-benchmark-lab.json
- Perf-canary integration: sources/linear/engineering/ENG-2456-integrate-mixed-workload-scenarios-into-perf-canary.json
- SRE guardrails: sources/linear/engineering/ENG-2463-sre-review-rollout-guardrails-for-new-scheduler.json
- Release plan: sources/linear/engineering/ENG-2470-release-plan-enable-scheduler-prototype-in-us-east-canary.json

Notes
- These thresholds are intended for prototype graduation and can be revisited for productization (multi-tenant QoS, customer-configurable tiers). For now, we prioritize reducing user-visible tail latency while avoiding throughput cliffs and preventing long-request starvation.
comments: 2026-01-10 (Lauren Bishop): Creating this to unblock ENG design review. We need crisp pass/fail thresholds before we can ask SRE to approve a canary ramp.

2026-01-14 (Nikhil Sharma): Drafted Hosted metrics proposal: prioritize p95 TTFT for short prompts (chat responsiveness). Added throughput guardrail at 3% for Hosted default pools; open to discussion if this is too strict.

2026-01-20 (Sean Gallagher): Please align “rollback triggers” with SRE doc; metrics are fine, but we need explicit tie-in to error budget and regional guardrails. Also define starvation event precisely so it can be alerted on.

2026-01-27 (Lena Fischer): Eng note: classification threshold may change per-model/SKU; please avoid hard-coding prompt token cutoff as the only reporting dimension. Reporting by runtime class labels + token buckets would work.

2026-02-03 (Lauren Bishop): Dedicated tolerance updated to allow up to 5% throughput regression if p95 improves; beyond that requires explicit approvals. This matches what we can reasonably discuss with Dedicated customers who care more about p95 than raw throughput.

2026-02-11 (Aisha Bello): Added suggestion for starvation definition based on long-class wait time vs baseline. We should also include a sustained condition (5+ min) to avoid false positives during load ramps.
2026-02-18 (Nikhil Sharma): Marking In Review. Next step: publish Confluence scorecard + confirm thresholds with Mateo/Sofia before ENG-2470 canary steps proceed.
